blocks.text: **The problem.** You are given an array of intervals, where `intervals[i] = [start, end]`. Merge all **overlapping** intervals and return the non-overlapping intervals that cover exactly the same ranges.

blocks.alt: Four intervals on a number line: [1,3], [2,6], [8,10] and [15,18]. The first two overlap and merge into [1,6]; the others stay as they are.

blocks.text: Example

blocks.code:
Input:  [[1,3], [2,6], [8,10], [15,18]]
Output: [[1,6], [8,10], [15,18]]      [1,3] and [2,6] overlap, so they become [1,6]

Input:  [[1,4], [4,5]]
Output: [[1,5]]                       touching intervals count as overlapping

blocks.text: Understanding the problem

Two intervals overlap when one starts **before (or exactly when) the other ends**. Merging them gives an interval from the earlier start to the **later** end. Think of meetings in a calendar: back-to-back or overlapping meetings merge into one busy block.
The input isn't sorted — the classic test case lists `[15, 18]` before `[2, 6]` — and that's what makes it feel hard at first.
Brute force

Compare every pair of intervals; whenever two overlap, replace them with their merge, and start over until nothing changes. Each round is O(n²) and there can be many rounds — slow, and fiddly to write correctly.
The key insight: sort by start

Sort the intervals by their start. Now any interval that could overlap the one you're building must come **right after it**: once an interval starts after the current end, every later interval starts even later, so none of them can reach back.

So after sorting, one pass is enough. Keep the last merged interval; for each next interval, either it **overlaps** (extend the end) or there's a **gap** (the last interval is final — start a new one).

blocks.alt: Snapshots of the merge pass over the sorted intervals [1,3], [2,6], [8,10], [15,18]. [2,6] overlaps [1,3] and stretches it to [1,6]. [8,10] starts after 6, so a new interval begins. [15,18] starts after 10, so another begins.

blocks.text: Why Math.max is essential

The obvious-looking `last.end = current.end` is wrong, and it fails on **nested** intervals. Take `[[1, 10], [2, 3]]`: they overlap, but `[2, 3]` sits entirely **inside** `[1, 10]`, so the merged end must stay 10 — not shrink to 3. `max(last.end, current.end)` handles it; plain assignment silently loses coverage.
Dry run it yourself
Enter intervals as `[start,end]` pairs in any order — the first step sorts them. Try the **Nested** example to watch `max` keep the end at 10.
Code

In Java, `Integer.compare(a[0], b[0])` is safer than `a[0] - b[0]`, which can overflow for very large or very negative values. In C++, sorting vectors compares them element by element, which sorts by start first.
Complexity

blocks.alt: Sorting dominates: O(n log n) time, and O(n) space for the output.

blocks.text: **Time: O(n log n)** — the sort dominates; the merge pass itself is O(n). **Space: O(n)** for the output (plus whatever the sort uses).
Edge cases to test
Where this idea shows up again

"Sort by start, then sweep once" is the backbone of this whole chapter: **inserting** a new interval into a sorted list, finding how many meeting rooms are needed, and finding the busiest moment all build on it.
